# Crystal detector and crystal radio (`crystal_detector`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by electromagnetic_waves_radio, telephone, ohms_law_circuits
- Core idea: Certain crystals pass current much more easily in one direction than in the other when touched by a fine metal point: galena (natural lead sulphide) with a springy bronze or steel wire, the cat's whisker, or silicon or carborundum with a steel point. Such a contact turns the rapid alternating current from a tuned aerial circuit into pulses in one direction that a sensitive earphone can follow. A long wire aerial, an earth connection, a coil of some 50 to 100 turns with a variable condenser, the crystal and a high-resistance earphone make a complete receiver that needs no battery, since all the power comes from the transmitter. The same one-way contact is the ancestor of the semiconductor diode and of the radar detectors of the Second World War.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting every spot on the crystal to work; the point must be moved until a sensitive spot is found, and a knock loses it
  - Using a low-resistance telephone receiver or a loudspeaker; only a sensitive receiver with thousands of turns of fine wire will sound
  - A short aerial or poor earth; with no amplification every microwatt counts
  - Thinking a crystal set can amplify; it only rectifies
- History: europe: 1874 – Ferdinand Braun finds one-way conduction at metal points on sulphide crystals (Leipzig); india: 1901 – J. C. Bose files a patent for a galena point-contact detector (granted in the United States in 1904); americas: 1906 – Pickard's silicon detector and Dunwoody's carborundum detector; crystal sets remain the common receiver into the 1920s
- Read:
  - Ferdinand Braun, Ueber die Stromleitung durch Schwefelmetalle, Annalen der Physik 229 (1875), 556–563
  - Sungook Hong, Wireless: From Marconi's Black-Box to the Audion (2001)
